title: Developer DX Playbook: One-Click SDK Scaffolds, Observability Recipes, and Triage Templates
author: Claire Nguyen
content:
Summary

This playbook bundles three cross-cutting deliverables for DX teams: 1) a one-click SDK scaffold for fast integration, 2) a set of opinionated observability recipes and dashboards tailored to Redwood inference patterns, and 3) canonical triage templates and remediation steps for the top support issues we see in the field. The goal is to reduce time-to-first-success for engineers integrating Redwood while making support outcomes predictable and auditable.

Scope

- SDK languages covered: JavaScript (Node), Python, and Go.
- Integration types: sync generation calls, streaming responses, embedding requests, and batched inference.
- Audience: SDK maintainers, developer advocates, solutions engineers, and L1/L2 support.

Owner and Contacts

- Playbook owner: DX Platform (eng-developer-experience).
- Primary contact: Claire Nguyen (author).
- Escalation: Miguel Alvarez (sdk-team) -> Priya Shah (sre).

1) Quickstart: One-Click SDK Scaffold

Purpose: a reproducible project scaffold with working examples for the four common integration patterns (sync, streaming, embeddings, batching). A single CLI command generates a repositorywith code, README, CI, and telemetry hooks.

Usage (CLI):

```
# install the DX scaffold generator
npm install -g redwood-dx-scaffold

# create a new Node quickstart using the hosted API and sample prompt set
redwood-scaffold create --lang node --integration streaming --auth api-key --name my-redwood-app
```

Scaffold contents (generated):

- README.md: step-by-step integration and configuration guidance.
- examples/: minimal examples for sync, streaming, embeddings, and batch invocation.
- telemetry/: example OpenTelemetry config + exporter shim to send to Redwood console.
- .github/workflows/ci.yml: lint, unit test, snippet validation.
- pr-template.md: integration checklist (see Templates).

Sample Node streaming snippet (generated):

```
const Redwood = require('@redwood/sdk');
const client = new Redwood.Client({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });

async function runStream() {
  const stream = await client.chat.stream({ model: 'r-instruct-1', messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Summarize product requirements' }] });
  for await (const chunk of stream) {
    process.stdout.write(chunk.text);
  }
}

runStream().catch(console.error);
```

Checklist included in README:

1. Create API key and set REDWOOD_API_KEY.
2. Run local emulator (see Docs site ops section) or use hosted endpoint.
3. Validate sample prompts with snippet validator: `npm run validate-snippets`.

2) Observability Recipes (metrics, traces, logs)

Design principle: metrics should be high-signal and low-cardinality by default; traces should capture request lifecycle across client -> network -> runtime -> model variant.

Mandatory metrics (recommended names and tags):

| Metric | Type | Labels/Tags | Thresholds / Alert hints |
|---|---:|---|---|
| redwood.request.count | counter | service,env,route,model,customer_id? | Alert: sudden >200% increase in 5m vs 30m baseline |
| redwood.request.latency_ms.p95 | gauge | service,env,route,model | SLO: p95 < 450ms for small-seq model routes |
| redwood.token.cost | gauge | model,quantization_profile | Alert: avg token cost > $0.005 per token for hosted tier |
| redwood.error.rate | ratio | service,env,route,error_code | Alert: error_rate > 0.5% sustained for 10m |

Span and trace guidance:

- Span names: redwood.client.request, redwood.runtime.schedule, redwood.runtime.kvcache.lookup, redwood.runtime.infer.
- Include the following attributes: request_id, model_name, seq_len_estimate, batching_key (if present), shard_id.
- Sampling: 1% global + 100% for requests with error_code >= 500 or latency > 2x SLO.

Log schema (JSON):

- timestamp (ISO8601), level, request_id, event, details (map-as-string), duration_ms, model_variant.

Example alert runbook (p95 latency breach):

1. Check redwood.request.latency_ms.p95 dashboard for affected routes.
2. Inspect traces filtered by trace attribute request_id or tag model_variant.
3. Verify autoscaling group metrics: GPU util, queue_size, batch_latency.
4. If queue_size > 50 for more than 2 minutes: increase autoscale target or apply burst capacity policy.
5. If model variant CPU/GPU kernel hot-path shows slow kernel (see runtime-telemetry): schedule model-rollforward to a lighter quantized variant.

3) Canonical Support Issues and Remediation Templates

Format for each issue: Summary, Symptoms, Root Causes (common), Triage steps, Quick fixes, Follow-up actions. Use the triage-ticket template in the issue tracker and link to the snippets used to reproduce.

Issue A: SDK hangs on streaming (client-side EOF not received)

- Symptoms: client receives partial content and stops; connection remains open; no final meta chunk.
- Common root causes: proxy/gateway (TLS idle timeout), incorrect client backpressure handling, runtime resource OOM.
- Triage steps:
  1. Reproduce with scaffold example and `REDWOOD_API_URL` pointed at the same endpoint.
  2. Capture tcpdump or use `curl --raw` to see if server is sending final chunk.
  3. Check client socket/window/backpressure logs; enable DEBUG logging in SDK.
  4. Inspect runtime logs for `stream.complete` event.
- Quick fixes:
  - Increase HTTP keepalive / timeout on gateway.
  - Upgrade SDK to latest streaming client which includes chunk-join fixes.
- Follow-up: add an automated snippet test that asserts final chunk is received within 10s.

Issue B: High token cost unexpectedly for a route

- Symptoms: finance alerts + customer complains of cost surge.
- Common root causes: prompt drift (longer prompts), unbounded sampling temperature, misconfigured batching (single-request batching disabled).
- Triage steps:
  1. Pull telemetry for `redwood.token.cost` by route for last 72h.
  2. Diff prompt-set golden vs current atlas using eval harness.
  3. Inspect SDK call parameters for `max_tokens` and `temperature`.
- Quick fixes:
  - Apply automatic truncation policy to prompt inputs.
  - Pin model to a cheaper quantized variant while investigating.
- Follow-up: create a regression test in the eval harness to detect prompt growth.

4) API Examples and Fault Patterns

Best-practice patterns included in scaffold: retries with jitter, idempotency keys for non-streaming generative calls, graceful fallback to smaller models, timeout orchestration that aligns client and runtime.

Example retry pattern (pseudo-code):

```
async function callWithRetry(payload) {
  const maxAttempts = 3;
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await client.generate(payload);
    } catch (e) {
      if (!isTransient(e) || attempt === maxAttempts) throw e;
      await sleep(jitteredBackoff(attempt));
    }
  }
}
```

Idempotency guidance:

- Non-streaming generation endpoints support Idempotency-Key header. Generate stable key on client when re-sending the same prompt (hash of prompt + user_id + context_version).

Batching guidance:

- Use the SDK batch helper to aggregate requests with similar seq_len_estimate and priority. Default batching window = 5ms for low-latency routes, 50ms for high-throughput.

5) Docs Site Operations: Snippet Validation and Publishing Checklist

Automated snippet validation is required for any public-facing code example. The scaffold includes `validate-snippets` which runs each snippet against the local emulator and ensures outputs match golden patterns.

Publishing checklist (developers must complete before merging docs):

1. Run `npm run validate-snippets` and attach results to PR.
2. Add snippet metadata (language, run-time requirements, redwood-sdk-version) to the example header.
3. If the snippet uses streaming, include a deterministic test harness that asserts chunk order.
4. For any new SDK-level API, add compatibility notes and migration instructions in the changelog.

6) Templates and Automation

Included templates (files created by scaffold and available in repo-templates/):

- pr-template.md (integration checklist)
- incident-template.md (triage fields mapped to Sentry and internal ticketing)
- rollback-playbook.md (how to revert canary and emergency model rollback)

Example PR checklist (top-level items):

- [ ] Snippets validated with local emulator.
- [ ] Tests added for streaming EOF receipt.
- [ ] Observability metrics added (metric names and tags).
- [ ] Docs site metadata included.

7) Canary and Rollout Patterns for SDK Changes

When releasing SDKs or changing default behavior (e.g., default batch window), follow a canary release pattern:

1. Publish a canary build (npm tag `canary`) and run the scaffold validation in the CI for 10% of CI jobs.
2. Enable canary feature flag for 5% of internal customers and monitor redwood.request.error_rate and redwood.request.latency_ms.p95.
3. After 72 hours with no regressions, promote to `latest`.

8) Ownership, SLOs, and Escalation

- SDK maintainers: 48-hour SLA to respond to critical regressions raised by support.
- DX Platform: weekly review of top 10 failing snippet tests.
- SRE: own alerts related to runtime latency breaches and autoscale behavior.

Related Documents and Artifacts

- SDK snippet validator (CI job): .github/workflows/snippet-validate.yml
- Local emulator image: docker.redwood-internal/emulators/redwood-local:2026-02
- Eval harness for prompt drift detection: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/prompt-drift-detector

Appendix: Example triage ticket fields (copy into ticket template)

- Title, Priority, Affected Route(s), Customer ID, SDK Version, Repro Steps, Logs (link), Trace IDs (link), Screenshot/Gist of request, First actions taken, Assigned owner, ETA for next update.

Notes and future work

- Add Rust and Java SDK scaffolds in H2 2026.
- Integrate snippet validation with the public docs site preview so broken snippets fail preview builds.
- Expand canary automation to include samples of real customer prompt sets (privacy redaction required).

End of document
